title: Compaction escrow and hazard window for graded KV revival
creator: Aisha Raman
description:
Summary:
Introduce two cooperating mechanisms to reduce repeated costly rehydrations and decoding stalls caused by aggressive eviction during high concurrency decode waves: (1) a lightweight 'compaction escrow' where recently-evicted fragments are retained in a compact, compressed buffer for fast graded revival, and (2) a short-duration 'hazard window' that temporarily protects freshly-prefilled fragments from eviction while their decode locality is still settling. Together these aim to reduce end-to-end tail latency, lower GPU memory churn, and improve token-per-dollar by avoiding full restores for fragments that are likely to be reused within a short temporal horizon.

Motivation / background:
- Observed pattern: under bursty traffic with interleaved multi-tenant workloads, we often evict recently prefetched KV fragments because of tight memory pressure, only to rehydrate them a few decoding steps later. That causes repeated decode stalls and extra memory writes.
- Current eviction is immediate or LRU-based without a short probation period, and our compaction pipeline is optimized for periodic background work rather than low-latency revival.
- We need a low-cost path to 'resurrect' an evicted fragment without performing a full disk/remote restore and decompression in the hot decode path.

Goals:
- Reduce median and 99th-percentile prefill/decode stall latency for paged-attention workloads by 10-25% in burst scenarios.
- Lower number of full rehydrations per decode session by 30-50% for sequences with high temporal locality.
- Keep extra memory overhead under 5% of a shard's working set on average; make escrow capacity configurable per-shard/tenant.

Design (high-level):
1) Compaction escrow:
   - When a fragment is selected for eviction from the regular KV pages, instead of immediately discarding it, we optionally move a compacted representation into a small in-memory escrow ring buffer per-shard. The compacted form trades a little CPU decompression cost for drastically less bytes (e.g., quantized deltas, run-length, or a micro-ledger encoding tuned for KV embeddings and attention keys/values).
   - Escrow entries are stored as contiguous compact blobs with a minimal header (fragment id, seq-range, approx decode-cost). They are kept for a short TTL (configurable, default 500ms) or until escrow pressure forces eviction.
   - Revival path: if the runtime needs a fragment that exists in escrow, it can perform a fast graded revival: a low-latency lightweight decode-path that reconstructs only the subset of tensor slices required for the immediate decode (rather than full rehydrate), and returns it to the hot shard with a short probation status.

2) Hazard window (probation period):
   - When a fragment is newly prefetched or revived from escrow, mark it with a hazard timestamp. For a short hazard window (configurable, e.g., 200-800ms depending on workload signatures), the fragment will not be chosen for eviction unless the shard is under extreme memory emergency (hard cap breach).
   - The hazard window is adaptive: we track short-term reuse rate and increase/decrease the window per fragment cohort. Cohorts are defined by sequence-length buckets, tenant weight, and kernel affinity.

3) Graded revival strategy and policies:
   - If a fragment is needed and present in escrow: perform graded revival (fast path) that reconstructs only requested token spans; if later accesses require additional spans, the revival can incrementally fill more slices. This prevents paying full restoration cost upfront when only a prefix is needed.
   - If not in escrow: fall back to normal restore (from remote storage or cold page).

Implementation plan / milestones:
- Spike (done) 2025-02-20: microbenchmark compact encodings (quantized delta vs simple RLE) across GLM/OPT-style KV shapes. Findings: a 6-12x size reduction for attention keys/values depending on sparsity; graded decode overhead ~1.2-1.6x CPU vs full restore but <10% of full remote restoration latency.
- Data model & wire: define escrow header and shard-level ring buffer metadata (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/11234 - spike).
- Engine changes (this ticket): integrate escrow buffer into eviction code path, implement graded revival APIs, hazard window tagging, and basic adaptive window heuristics.
- Testing & perf harness: add synthetic bursty workload test cases in the runtime perf suite, and a chaos test that forces churn to validate safety. (Perf harness PR TBD).
- Rollout: feature gate behind runtime-1.26 flag; default off for new Dedicated clusters, opt-in for internal canary.

Metrics to measure:
- revive_hit_rate = revivals_from_escrow / total_fragment_requests (target > 30% for bursty patterns)
- reduction_in_full_rehydrates = compare baseline full restores per minute (target -30% to -50%)
- prefill_decode_tail_latency P99 before/after (target -10%-25%)
- escrow_memory_overhead percent per shard (target < 5%)
- CPU overhead for graded revival (target < +5% overall CPU for shard under normal load)

Backward compatibility & safety:
- Escrow is opt-in per-shard and bounded; we will never exceed a configured escrow cap. If the runtime has strict isolation requirements (Private deployments), escrow can be disabled.
- Hazard window honoring is conservative: only prevents eviction when normal eviction heuristics would otherwise evict; in emergency, eviction will still force out hazard entries.

Alternatives considered and why rejected:
- Keep everything in LRU but tune time constants: insufficient because rehydrations are expensive and tuning cannot avoid repeated full restores.
- Write-through lightweight local SSD staging area for evicted fragments: adds I/O costs and complicates deployment for Private on-prem customers.
- Aggressive prefill trimming (only fetch prefixes): useful independently but still triggers rehydrates when longer spans are needed; compaction escrow complements prefix prefill.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Optimal compact format: we need one format that generalizes across model families; spike suggests two-tier formats (fast small compact for keys, heavier for values). Decision TBD with Research team.
- Hazard window tuning: per-tenant vs global heuristics—initial approach is cohort-based and conservative.
- Cost model: graded revival uses more CPU than immediate restore from warm pages; need to validate cost/performance on production traffic.

Risks:
- Additional CPU on revive hot path could increase contention if not throttled.
- Incorrect compact encoding could subtly affect numeric fidelity for quantized tensors; requires thorough validation in eval harness.
